opus-5.5.text:
I think the right answer is that the standard should depend on what the writing is for, and especially on who bears the cost when the model gets something wrong.

If I'm using an LLM to help me brainstorm, draft a short story, or write a toast for a friend's wedding, a hallucination isn't really a failure. In creative contexts, the ability to make things up is the point. The bar is basically: is it useful, is it interesting, does it sound like me? Nobody is harmed if the model invents a detail about a fictional character.

At the other end of the spectrum you have writing that people will rely on as factual: a legal brief, a medical summary, a news article, a scientific paper, even a business report that will drive decisions. There the tolerance for fabrication should be very close to zero. We've all seen the cases of lawyers submitting briefs with invented case citations. That isn't a quirky failure, it's a real harm, and it erodes trust in the whole system.

In between is a big gray zone, things like drafting an email, summarizing a meeting, or writing marketing copy. There I think the standard is less about the model alone and more about the workflow. Is there a human in the loop who knows the facts and will check the output? If so, you can tolerate a higher rate of errors from the model, because the system as a whole, human plus machine, is what needs to be reliable.

So in research terms I'd frame it less as one hallucination rate and more as context-dependent error tolerance, much like we think about fairness or privacy. There's no universal threshold. You have to specify the use case, the stakeholders, and the cost of different kinds of mistakes, and then ask whether the system meets that bar. It also argues for models that are better calibrated, that can signal when they're uncertain or when they're generating rather than retrieving. That would let users apply the right standard themselves, rather than treating every output with the same level of trust or suspicion.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts creative writing with factual journalism, but does not specifically address historical fiction.

r002.rationale: It does not say that historical fiction needs to remain aligned with real historical facts.

r003.rationale: It says that in creative contexts, including fiction, making things up is the point and a hallucination is not really a failure.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the first thing to say is that "hallucination" is a bit of an overloaded term, and the whole premise of your question is right, which is that there isn't a single standard. It really depends on what the writing is for and what the cost of a false statement is in that context.

So let me give you the extremes. If I'm using an LLM to help me draft a short story or a poem or a wedding toast, the notion of hallucination almost doesn't apply. There's no ground truth. If the model invents a character or a plot twist, that's not an error, that's the feature. We don't say a novelist hallucinated.

At the other extreme, if I'm using it to draft a legal brief, or a medical summary, or a scientific paper with citations, then the standard has to be essentially zero tolerance for fabricated facts. And we've already seen the famous cases, the lawyers who filed briefs with cases that didn't exist. In those settings a single fabricated citation can be disqualifying, not because the rest of the document was bad, but because it destroys trust in the whole artifact. The reader can no longer tell which parts to believe.

And then there's this big middle ground, which is where most writing actually happens. Emails, marketing copy, blog posts, a summary of a meeting. And there I think the right way to think about it is less about a fixed threshold and more about who bears the responsibility for verification, and how easy that verification is. If I'm drafting an email and the model inserts a claim about when the meeting is, I'm going to read it before I send it, I know when the meeting is, and the cost of catching the error is very low. If it's generating a three-thousand-word report full of statistics that I'd have to go look up individually, the verification burden is high, and so the standard for the model should be correspondingly higher, or it should be forced to show its sources.

So the thing I'd push on is that the standard isn't just a property of the model, it's a property of the model plus the workflow plus the human in the loop. The same model with the same error rate might be perfectly fine in one pipeline and dangerous in another. And honestly, from the machine learning side, I think we'd be better off thinking about this the way we think about any other error rate with asymmetric costs. There are domains where a false positive is cheap and a false negative is expensive, and vice versa, and we tune accordingly. Hallucination should be treated the same way rather than as a single scalar that we're trying to drive to zero everywhere.

The last thing I'd say is that what we really want, and what we mostly don't have yet, is calibration. A model that could reliably say "I'm confident about this sentence and not that one" would let the standard vary almost automatically, because the human could allocate their attention to the uncertain parts. That, to me, is more promising than just trying to reduce the global rate.

r001.rationale: It says hallucination is largely inapplicable to fiction, but does not compare historical fiction with journalism or state that fiction has higher tolerance.

r002.rationale: It does not say that historical fiction must align with actual historical facts.

r003.rationale: It says that for a short story there is no ground truth and that inventing characters or plot twists is a feature, so hallucination almost does not apply.

astra-6.text:
I think it depends very much on what you’re asking it to write. If you’re using an LLM to help write a short story, making things up is part of the assignment. You might care about whether the story is internally consistent, but you don’t need every event or character to correspond to something in the real world.

If you’re asking it to write a scientific literature review, that’s a very different situation. A plausible-sounding citation to a paper that doesn’t exist is a serious failure. And even if all the papers exist, you still need to know whether it’s accurately representing what they say.

So I wouldn’t want a single standard for hallucination across all writing tasks. I’d ask: Which parts of this task are supposed to be grounded in facts? What are the consequences of getting those facts wrong? And how will somebody check them? You can give the system a lot of freedom in how it expresses something while still demanding accuracy in what it asserts.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts short stories with scientific literature reviews, but does not compare historical fiction with journalism.

r002.rationale: It says short-story events and characters need not correspond to reality; it does not require historical fiction to align with historical facts.

r003.rationale: It says that making things up is part of writing a short story and that its events and characters need not correspond to reality, suggesting hallucination may not apply to pure fiction.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it depends very much on what you’re asking it to write. If you’re asking for a short story, making things up is part of the task. You might care about internal consistency, but you’re not asking whether those events actually happened. If you’re asking it to help write a scientific paper or summarize a legal document, then inventing a citation or a fact is a very different kind of failure.

And even within one writing task, you might want different standards. You can give the model considerable freedom in how it expresses an idea while insisting that the factual claims be grounded in material you’ve supplied. So I don’t think there’s a single hallucination rate that’s acceptable across applications. The standard should reflect what the reader is going to rely on and what the consequences are if something is wrong.
